narrative:
The model predicted an 82.9% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence; being in the bottom decile (compared to an average of roughly the sixth decile among accepted students) strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your first-year ranking was the second most important factor and also pulled the outcome toward failure, as you placed in the second decile while accepted students averaged the sixth. Your undergraduate GPA was the third most influential piece of information, but it worked in the opposite direction: although your 2.6 GPA is noticeably below the 3.23 average of accepted students, this value actually made the model slightly less pessimistic about your chances.

Taken together, the model saw your consistently low class standing as clear evidence that you would struggle with the bar exam, outweighing the modest positive signal from your GPA.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record and bar-exam readiness. Consider retaking key courses, enrolling in a structured bar-preparation program, or gaining additional legal experience before reapplying. These steps can directly address the areas that most hurt your prediction. (218 words)
